query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: Near-equiatomic, single‐phase high-entropy nanoparticles remain chemically and structurally stable at elevated catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) service temperatures because their high configurational entropy and associated lattice distortions severely slow atomic diffusion and hinder phase segregation.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles synthesized to achieve a single-phase structure with high chemical disorder and lattice distortion.
generation.intervention: Prepare two sets of nanoparticles: one with near-equiatomic compositions (maximizing configurational entropy) and a second set with slight off-stoichiometric deviations (reduced configurational entropy). Then subject both sets to extended high-temperature aging under controlled (inert or low-oxygen) environments.
generation.conditions: High-temperature catalytic environments (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric operating regimes (473–1923 K) under atmospheres that minimize oxidation (e.g., inert gas or controlled oxygen partial pressure).
generation.structural_mediator: The local lattice distortions and high density of atomic-scale defects (chemical disorder) that kinetically trap atoms in a disordered, single-phase structure.
generation.mechanism: The high configurational entropy inherent to near-equiatomic compositions forces severe lattice distortions, which increases kinetic barriers for atomic diffusion. This suppression of diffusion prevents phase segregation and coarsening of the nanoparticles at high temperatures, maintaining both the structural integrity and the uniform distribution of multiple elements.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with maximized configurational entropy will retain their single-phase structure and homogeneous composition during high-temperature service, whereas off-stoichiometric nanoparticles will show signs of phase decomposition, chemical segregation, and increased grain growth relative to the near-equiatomic baseline.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles evaluated immediately post-synthesis under ambient conditions, and near-equiatomic nanoparticles that have not been exposed to prolonged high-temperature regimes.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies when the nanoparticles are synthesized as single-phase, near-equiatomic solid solutions and the high-temperature environment does not introduce substantial oxidizing conditions. If multi-phase formation or oxidation dominates the degradation process, the kinetic trapping provided by high configurational entropy may not be sufficient to ensure stability.
generation.uncertainty: The precise compositional tolerances and temperature thresholds at which the kinetic barriers fail to prevent diffusion and phase segregation are not yet quantitatively defined and require systematic study.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two groups of nanoparticles: one group with a strict near-equiatomic composition and a second group with slight compositional deviations that lower the overall configurational entropy. Subject both groups to identical prolonged high-temperature aging processes under inert or controlled environments. Characterize the samples before and after aging using techniques such as X-ray diffraction (XRD), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS).
measurements: Phase identification via XRD to detect any emergence of secondary phases.
Morphological and grain size analysis via TEM.
Chemical mapping via EDS/XPS to assess elemental segregation or diffusion.
Comparative analysis of defect densities if possible.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the near-equiatomic and the off-stoichiometric nanoparticles show similar extents of phase degradation, chemical inhomogeneity, or particle coarsening after aging, this would falsify the hypothesis that high configurational entropy (and its induced lattice distortion) is the dominant factor governing nanoparticle stability under service conditions.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted much attention in various fields with regard to applications as structural materials, biomaterials, supercapacitors, and catalysts., HEAs comprise mixtures of five or more metallic elements at near equiatomic ratios and form simple single solid-solution phases having lattice structures including face-centered cubic (fcc) and body-centered cubic (bcc)., The high configurational entropy of these alloys stabilizes the solid-solution phase such that this phase appears rather than an intermetallic phase or phase segregation., The severe lattice distortion in these materials that results from differences in the atomic sizes of the constituent elements also causes low atomic diffusivity. The unique synergistic effects resulting from combining multiple elements provide high specific strength, ductility, corrosion resistance, and thermal stability, such that HEAs are unique and fascinating materials. In recent years, many researchers have reported that HEA nanoparticles (NPs) having sizes on the nanometer scale (that is, in the range of 1 to 100 nm) show promise with regard to catalytic applications. High-entropy oxides (HEOs) have aroused growing interest due to fundamental questions relating to their structure formation, phase stability, and the interplay between configurational disorder and physical and chemical properties. Introducing Fe(II) and Mn(II) into a rocksalt HEO is considered challenging, as theoretical analysis suggests that they are unstable in this structure under ambient conditions. Here, we develop a bottom-up method for synthesizing Mn- and Fe-containing rocksalt HEO (FeO-HEO). We present a comprehensive investigation of its crystal structure and the random cation-site occupancy. We show the improved structural robustness of this FeO-HEO and verify the viability of an oxygen sublattice as a buffer layer. Compositional analysis reveals the valence and spin state of the iron species. We further report the antiferromagnetic order of this FeO-HEO below the transition temperature ~218 K and predict the conditions of phase stability of Mn- and Fe-containing HEOs. Our results provide fresh insights into the design and property tailoring of emerging classes of HEOs. In nanomaterial science, developing methods for the rapid and reliable synthesis of nanoparticles, especially from complex materials like HEAs, is essential [,]. HEAs, with their composition of four or more principal elements in nearly equal molar ratios, have significantly altered the traditional approach to alloy design. These alloys are distinguished by their diverse multi-element composition, leading to an array of desirable physicochemical and mechanical properties [,]. Their versatile application potential spans a range of industries, including high-temperature materials, anti-corrosion, electrocatalysis, advanced welding, and brazing [,,,,]. The real power of HEAs lies in their high-entropy effect, which promotes the formation of simple solid phases over a more intermetallic composition, thereby granting these alloys remarkable characteristics. In our study, we selected an HEA composed of CuCoMn1.75NiFe0.25 due to its potential catalytic properties stemming from its composition, its effectiveness in brazing and welding applications, and the high probability of being single phase [,,,,,].
